table.text: In our primary 12-week analysis, we had 80% power to detect cumulative rate ratios of approximately 1.16 for TB and 1.14 for NTM per SD of activity. The null estimates we identified therefore argue against a large population-level effect but do not exclude a clinically important individual-level effect in a smaller subgroup. The TB point estimate below 1 should not be interpreted as protective, but an incidence rate ratio below 1 may suggest that viral surges could have delayed TB diagnosis and attenuated a short-term association. Analyses extending the maximum lag to 26 and 52 weeks also detected no association, arguing against a delayed effect at the population level.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Background: Tuberculosis (TB) notifications have increased in several high-income countries since 2020.
Proposed explanations include pandemic-related disruption of treatment for latent tuberculosis, changes in population composition, and immune dysfunction following SARS-CoV-2 infection.
We assessed whether TB presentations increased during the pandemic era and then tested whether community SARS-CoV-2 activity was followed by increased mycobacterial disease.

We conducted a population-based ecological time-series study of first TB-and nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM)-coded hospital, emergency-department and ambulatory-clinic presentations in the Greater Toronto-Hamilton Area Plus (GTHA+), Ontario (2024 population approximately 11.2 million), from April 2011 through March 2024.
NTM served as a comparator because it shares diagnostic pathways with TB but differs epidemiologically.
Negative-binomial projection and full-series models estimated pandemic-era changes under three alternative trend assumptions.
Distributed lag nonlinear models estimated cumulative rate ratios for standardized community viral activity over 0-12 weeks; sensitivity analyses extended the maximum lag to 26 and 52 weeks.

Influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) were prespecified comparators; data for five additional viral exposures were obtained after the primary analysis was completed and analysed as exploratory comparisons.
Results: We identified 3,985 first TB-coded and 5,214 first NTM-coded acute-care presentations.
Across six models, estimated pandemic-era TB increases ranged from 3% to 22%.
No model suggested an increased in NTM.
SARS-CoV-2 activity was not.

Tuberculosis (TB) notifications have increased since 2020 in several high-income countries, including the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada (1-6); the Canadian incidence rate rose from 5.1 per 100,000 population in 2019 to 6.1 per 100,000 in 2024, corresponding to an increase from 1,921 to 2,508 reported cases (3) (4) (5).

text.text: Several mechanisms could produce a SARS-CoV-2 pandemic-era increase in TB, including disruption of TB prevention and diagnostic services (7, 8), delayed diagnosis, changes in population composition and healthcare use, and immune effects following SARS-CoV-2 infection.

text.text: Acquired immunological abnormalities have been reported following SARS-CoV-2 infection (9) (10) (11) (12) (13) (14).
text.formatted: Acquired immunological abnormalities have been reported following SARS-CoV-2 infection <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref>.

text.text: As control of latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection depends heavily on cell-mediated immunity, post-infectious immune dysfunction could plausibly have contributed to observed pandemic-era increases in TB.
Determining whether TB presentations exceeded expectations during the pandemic requires careful evaluation of pre-pandemic trends and seasonality.
However, identifying an increase beyond expectations does not, in itself, establish its cause.
If such an increase resulted from immune effects of SARS-CoV-2 infection, surges in SARS-CoV-2 activity would be expected to be followed by increased TB presentations.
By contrast, service disruption, migration, changes in healthcare use, or ascertainment could alter the pandemic-era level without tracking short-term viral activity.
Nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) disease shares laboratory diagnostic pathways with TB but has different epidemiological and immunological determinants (15) (16) (17) (18).
text.formatted: Nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) disease shares laboratory diagnostic pathways with TB but has different epidemiological and immunological determinants <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref>.

text.text: NTM are environmental organisms acquired from water and soil rather than from other people, so . that NTM disease does not propagate through transmission chains and is not subject to the contact tracing and preventive therapy that shape TB epidemiology.
Pulmonary disease predominates and presents indolently, with chronic cough, sputum production and weight loss developing over months.

Risk is governed largely by airway architecture, with bronchiectasis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease the dominant predisposing conditions and a substantial burden among older women with structural lung disease (15) (16) (17); cell-mediated immune competence, which is central to control of latent M. tuberculosis infection, is a far less important determinant outside rare syndromes of Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (15) (16) (17) (18).

text.text: NTM presentations therefore provide a useful comparator, and convergence or divergence in secular trends and associations with viral activity may be informative.

Using population-based administrative data for approximately 11 million Ontario residents over 13 years, we evaluated whether first TB-and NTM-coded acute-care presentations departed from pre-pandemic trajectories.

We then tested whether weekly SARS-CoV-2 activity predicted subsequent presentations over maximum lag windows of 12, 26, and 52 weeks; whether associations differed by age or recorded immunocompromising condition; and how the results compared with those for other respiratory viruses.

We conducted a population-based ecological time-series study of first tuberculosis (TB)-and nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM)-coded health care presentations (hospital admissions, emergency-department [ED] visits and visits to selected ambulatory clinics) in the Greater Toronto-Hamilton Area Plus (GTHA+), Ontario.

The catchment comprised 14 public health units covering approximately 5% of Ontario's land area and had a combined 2024 population of approximately 11.2 million, representing about 70% of Ontario's and 27% of Canada's populations (Supplementary Appendix).
The outcome series extended from April 1, 2011, through March 31, 2024 (676 analyzed weeks).
The 468 weeks through March 14, 2020, constituted the prepandemic period; the pandemic era began March 15, 2020, with the onset of community SARS-CoV-2 transmission in Ontario.
For lagged analyses, observations preceding the analytic period were used only to construct exposure histories and did not contribute outcome observations.

We ascertained weekly counts of first TB-and NTM-coded acute-care presentations from two linked Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI) administrative databases: the Discharge Abstract Database for acute inpatient admissions and the National Ambulatory Care Reporting System for emergency-department visits and for visits to selected ambulatory clinics, including family medicine clinics.
TB was defined by ICD-10-CA codes A15, A17, A18, or A19 in any diagnosis field; A16, which denotes clinically suspected but unconfirmed pulmonary TB, was excluded as nonspecific.
NTM disease was defined by code A31.

We linked records using encrypted health-card numbers and retained the earliest observed qualifying record for each person separately for TB and NTM; a person could therefore contribute once to each outcome.
This yielded 3,985 first TB-coded and 5,214 first NTM-coded presentations.

Because these outcomes were administrative health care records rather than validated publichealth notifications, and because the ambulatory component is not restricted to unscheduled care, we describe them as health care presentations rather than incident cases.

Recorded immunocompromising host conditions (ICH) comprised HIV/AIDS (B20-B24, Z21), solid-organ transplantation (Z940-Z944), stem-cell or marrow transplantation (Z941, Z948), haematological malignancy (C81-C85, C88, C90-C96), or primary immunodeficiency (D80-D84).
Medication-induced immunosuppression was not reliably captured; some affected people could therefore have been classified as not having a recorded ICH.

Given changes in data collection, SARS-CoV-2 activity was represented by a composite series spanning two surveillance periods: test-adjusted case counts from Ontario's Case and Contact Management System from March 2020 through August 2022, corrected for differential testing intensity using a previously described method (19) (20) (21) Pre-specified analyses focused on SARS-CoV-2, influenza A/B viruses, and RSV, but we also conducted exploratory analyses for five additional respiratory-virus groups (human parainfluenza virus, human metapneumovirus, adenovirus, enterovirus/rhinovirus, and seasonal coronaviruses) for which data were available from September 2015 onward, and for which time series were obtained after our primary prespecified analysis had been completed.

text.text: To express associations on a common scale while preserving a meaningful zero, each exposure was divided by its SD over the period in which its surveillance metric was used, without mean-centring; the two components of the SARS-CoV-2 series were scaled before concatenation.
Zero therefore continued to represent no detected activity.
We indexed and merged exposure, outcome, and population series by calendar week using one-to-one date keys and checked for duplicate dates and unmatched weeks.
We first assessed whether mycobacterial presentations during the pandemic differed from the numbers expected from pre-pandemic patterns.
Negative-binomial models with Fourier terms for seasonality and a population offset were fitted to 468 available pre-pandemic weeks.
We used three representations of the underlying time trend (no trend, a linear trend, or a natural spline with 3 degrees of freedom) and projected expected weekly counts through the pandemic period.
For each model, an intercept-only negative-binomial model with the log expected count as an offset estimated the observed-to-expected rate ratio.
We also calculated cumulative excess presentations by summing weekly observed minus expected counts from March 15, 2020, onward.
As a complementary analysis, we used all 676 available weeks and estimated an average pandemic-era change while adjusting for the same seasonal and time-trend terms.

Model fit was compared using the Akaike and Bayesian information criteria within each approach and outcome, but all six estimates, three from the projection approach and three from the full-series approach, were reported.
Confidence intervals from the projection analysis treat expected counts as fixed and therefore omit some uncertainty about what would have happened in the absence of the pandemic.
We therefore considered whether findings were consistent across plausible trend assumptions rather than relying on any one model.

We next modelled temporal associations between viral activity and mycobacterial presentations using distributed lag non-linear models (DLNM) with a linear exposureresponse function and a natural-spline lag function with 3 degrees of freedom over a primary 0-12-week window (24).

text.text: Models used quasi-Poisson errors, a population offset, first-and second-order Fourier terms for seasonality, and a natural spline for continuous weekly time with 13 degrees of freedom over the 13-year series.
We report cumulative rate ratios per 1-SD increase in viral activity over the full lag window, together with lagspecific estimates.
Sensitivity analyses extended the maximum lag for SARS-CoV-2 to 26 and 52 weeks.
We repeated the primary SARS-CoV-2 analysis by age (<65 and ≥65 years) and recorded ICH status and used Wald tests to assess between-stratum heterogeneity.

text.text: Influenza and RSV were analysed using the same specification; all non-SARS-CoV-2 models were adjusted for concurrent SARS-CoV-2 activity.
The five additional respiratory-virus groups were analysed over the shorter period for which they were available.
These models assess whether weekly rises and falls in viral activity were followed by changes in mycobacterial presentations after accounting for seasonality and long-term trends.
Unlike the pre-pandemic projection analyses, they do not require estimating expected counts in the absence of the pandemic.
This study used de-identified administrative data in the CIHI Secure Access Environment and was approved by the Research Ethics Board of the University of Toronto (Protocol # 41690).

text.text: Over 13 years, we identified 3,985 first TB-coded and 5,214 first NTM-coded acute-care presentations, corresponding to crude rates of 2.86 and 3.75 per 100,000 person-years, respectively (Table 1).

text.text: Recorded ICH was present in 6.3% of TB and 13.5% of NTM presentations.
Adults aged 65 years or older had higher adjusted rates of both outcomes than those younger than 20 years (TB rate ratio 2.81; NTM rate ratio 5.87), and male sex was associated with TB but not NTM.
Crude pandemic-era rates were lower than pre-pandemic rates for both TB (2.70 vs 2.96 per 100,000 person-years) and NTM (3.26 vs 4.03).
Estimates of pandemic-era change depended on how expected counts in the absence of the pandemic were modelled, so we report both pre-pandemic projection and full-series analyses (Table 2; Figure 2).
text.formatted: Estimates of pandemic-era change depended on how expected counts in the absence of the pandemic were modelled, so we report both pre-pandemic projection and full-series analyses (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">2</ref>).

text.text: Under the three projection models, TB rate ratios were 1.095 (1.037-1.156) with seasonality alone, 1.067 (1.010-1.127) with a linear trend, and 1.031 (0.976-1.089) with a 3-degree-of-freedom natural spline.
Under the corresponding full-series models, estimates were 1.095 (1.022-1.174), 1.074 (0.955-1.209), and 1.217 (1.035-1.431).
All six point estimates exceeded unity, four confidence intervals excluded unity, and the estimated increase ranged from 3% to 22%.
Model-selection criteria did not identify a single preferred assumption.

The Bayesian information criterion favoured the no-trend models, both of which estimated a rate ratio of 1.095, while the Akaike information criterion favoured the spline models, which estimated 1.031 under projection and 1.217 in the full-series analysis.
Depending on the model, the estimates implied approximately 40-280 excess TBcoded presentations over four years.
Under the projection models, cumulative excess increased through early 2022 and then levelled off, ending between 41 and 119 cumulative excess presentations (Figure 2B).

text.text: This pattern was not consistent with a constant increase throughout the four-year pandemic period.
For NTM, all six pandemic-era estimates were at or below unity.

Projectionmodel rate ratios were 0.973 (0.924-1.025) with seasonality alone, 0.581 (0.552-0.612) with a linear trend, and 0.959 (0.910-1.011) with a 3-degree-of-freedom natural spline; the corresponding full-series estimates were 0.972 (0.905-1.045), 0.599 (0.537-0.667), and 0.849 (0.735-0.980).
The linear models produced the largest apparent deficits because they continued the steep pre-pandemic increase into the pandemic era.
No model suggested an increase, but the size of any decrease was uncertain.

Cumulative SARS-CoV-2 activity over 0-12 weeks was not positively associated with TB-coded presentations (cumulative rate ratio per 1-SD increase 0.909, 95% CI 0.822-1.006) or NTM-coded presentations (0.953, 0.868-1.047) (Figure 3; Supplementary Table S1).

text.text: No lag-specific estimate showed a statistically significant positive association.

Extending the maximum lag to 26 or 52 weeks did not reveal a positive cumulative association for either outcome (at 26 weeks, TB 0.897, 95% CI 0.746-1.078; NTM 0.862, 0.726-1.023; at 52 weeks, TB 0.639, 95% CI 0.318-1.281; NTM 1.233, 0.649-2.344).

Age-and recorded-ICH-stratified estimates were similar to the overall results, with no evidence of heterogeneity by age (TB p=0.941; NTM p=0.787) or recorded ICH status (TB p=0.776; NTM p=0.072) (Supplementary Table S1).

text.text: In this population-based study, TB-coded acute-care presentations were probably modestly elevated during the pandemic era, but we could not attribute these increases to direct effects of SARS-CoV-2 activity, at lags up to 52 weeks.
The estimated magnitude of the pandemic-era TB increase depended on how we represented what would have happened without the pandemic.

Models that projected pre-pandemic patterns beyond 2020 and models that estimated an average pandemic-era change from the full series produced estimates of different magnitudes because they made different assumptions about the underlying trend in cases.

A flexible trend can also behave differently when extended beyond 2020 than when fitted to the entire series, which is why our two approachs to estimating the effect of the pandemic on disease trends diverge most where splines were included in our models.
However, the consistent direction across all models supports an increase, whereas the 3%-22% range in this increase conveys the uncertainty more clearly than any single selected estimate.
We evaluated SARS-CoV-2 effects on mycobacterial disease risk at a population level by treating viral activity as an ecological exposure.
This approach has the advantage of not being subject to biases related to differential SARS-CoV-2 testing probability in individuals with medical comorbidity.
However, population-and individual-level relative risks may be quite different in magnitude, even for an identical individual-level effect.
A population time-series estimate applies to the entire population, although only a fraction of that population has been recently infected.
A large individuallevel effect confined to a small subgroup may therefore produce only a modest population-level association.

We recently demonstrated this distinction for pulmonary embolism: an Ontario time-series analysis found a 12% increase per SD of SARS-CoV-2 activity, whereas a Swedish individual-level study reported a greater than 30-fold increase following infection (25, 26).
text.formatted: We recently demonstrated this distinction for pulmonary embolism: an Ontario time-series analysis found a 12% increase per SD of SARS-CoV-2 activity, whereas a Swedish individual-level study reported a greater than 30-fold increase following infection <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">26)</ref>.

text.text: A similar dilution could occur for TB if elevated risk were concentrated among people with severe COVID-19 or particular vulnerabilities.

A nationwide Chilean cohort of 3.6 million adults, excluding those with recognized immunocompromise, found that severe COVID-19 was associated with a markedly increased risk of incident TB that peaked within the first six months and was attenuated by prior SARS-CoV-2 vaccination (27).
text.formatted: A nationwide Chilean cohort of 3.6 million adults, excluding those with recognized immunocompromise, found that severe COVID-19 was associated with a markedly increased risk of incident TB that peaked within the first six months and was attenuated by prior SARS-CoV-2 vaccination <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(27)</ref>.

text.text: Baseline latent and subclinical TB status was unavailable, however, and the study could not distinguish effects of severe infection from those of treatment, detection, or underlying vulnerability.
In our primary 12-week analysis, we had 80% power to detect cumulative rate ratios of approximately 1.16 for TB and 1.14 for NTM per SD of activity.
The null estimates we identified therefore argue against a large population-level effect but do not exclude a clinically important individual-level effect in a smaller subgroup.

The TB point estimate below 1 should not be interpreted as protective, but an incidence rate ratio below 1 may suggest that viral surges could have delayed TB diagnosis and attenuated a short-term association.
Analyses extending the maximum lag to 26 and 52 weeks also detected no association, arguing against a delayed effect at the population level.
Influenza and RSV were included in our analysis a priori to assess whether an anticipated SARS-CoV-2 association was virus-specific or reflected patterns shared across respiratory-virus seasons.

Contrary to this expectation, SARS-CoV-2 and influenza were not positively associated with either outcome, whereas RSV was positively associated with TB and NTM; adenovirus was also nominally associated with TB.
Only the RSV-NTM association remained after Bonferroni correction.
Correlated seasonality, changes in healthcare contact, and diagnostic opportunity could produce noncausal associations.

However, respiratory viruses can also have important immunological effects, and genuine virus-specific effects on mycobacterial disease are biologically plausible (28), and our ecological design cannot distinguish these possibilities.
text.formatted: However, respiratory viruses can also have important immunological effects, and genuine virus-specific effects on mycobacterial disease are biologically plausible <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(28)</ref>, and our ecological design cannot distinguish these possibilities.

text.text: The comparison is also not symmetric in precision: influenza and RSV were observed over the full thirteen years and across many epidemic cycles, whereas the SARS-CoV-2 series spans only the four years from 2020 and a smaller number of distinct waves, so the prespecified comparators were estimated from considerably more information.
Rather than providing the anticipated specificity test for SARS-CoV-2, these findings generate hypotheses concerning other respiratory viruses that require investigation using individual-level data.
While we identify a pandemic-era TB increase in central Ontario similar to that reported in other jurisdictions (1, 2, 5, 6), we are unable to resolve its cause.

NTM presentations did not show a corresponding increase, possibly because reductions in elective imaging, bronchoscopy, and respiratory cultures reduced ascertainment of pulmonary NTM early in the pandemic.

text.text: The Greater Toronto-Hamilton Area Plus (GTHA+) comprises 14 Public Health Units (PHUs) in central Ontario, Canada (Figure S1).

text.text: The region consists of the 6 PHUs of the Greater Toronto-Hamilton Area (Toronto, Hamilton, Peel, York, Durham, and Halton), plus 8 bordering PHUs: Simcoe-Muskoka, Haliburton-Kawartha-Pine Ridge, Peterborough, Wellington-Dufferin-Guelph, Waterloo, Brant, Niagara, and Haldimand-Norfolk.
The GTHA+ was selected to provide a large population concentrated in a relatively small geographic area, improving the relevance of common ecological exposure series.
The region represents approximately 70% of Ontario's population and 27% of Canada's population while comprising about 5% of Ontario's land area.
Its concentration of healthcare institutions also improves statistical precision for acute-care outcomes.
Population estimates for each PHU were obtained from Statistics Canada, which provides annual figures for both census and non-census years.
As of 2024, the GTHA+ had an estimated population of 11.2 million residents.
The region experienced substantial growth during the study period, with overall population increasing 41.3% between 2001 and 2024 (Figure S2).

To explore whether two candidate mechanisms could plausibly account for the TB excess, we developed an interactive scenario tool in which readers can vary literature-informed assumptions concerning disruption of latent-TB care and migration (https://fismanda.github.io/mycobacteria-and-respiratory-viruses/; archived at DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22216420).
The tool assesses order-of-magnitude plausibility rather than causal attribution.

Strengths of this study include its large, geographically concentrated population; long pre-pandemic baseline; separate evaluation of the pandemic-era increase and its hypothesized relationship with SARS-CoV-2 activity; sensitivity analyses extending the lag window to one year; and presentation of results under several assumptions about how pre-pandemic trends would have continued.

Important limitations are the ecological nature of viral exposure, absence of individual data on infection severity, vaccination, migration history, and subclinical TB, and use of a composite SARS-CoV-2 exposure spanning two surveillance systems.

Outcomes were first health care presentations identified through administrative codes rather than validated TB or NTM diagnoses or surveillance notifications, and because the ambulatory records available to us could not be separated into emergency and clinic encounters we could not restrict the outcome to unscheduled care, medication-induced immunosuppression could not be captured, and the size of immune compromised strata was small.
NTM was analysed as a composite outcome despite comprising clinically heterogeneous conditions with different anatomical and immunological determinants.

In conclusion, TB-coded acute-care presentations appear to have increased modestly during the pandemic era in central Ontario, Canada, but community SARS-CoV-2 activity was not positively associated with subsequent TB or NTM presentations over lag windows from 12 weeks to one year, and did not appear to explain the population-level TB increase.

Clinically important individual-level effects remain possible, particularly after severe COVID-19, and would require studies linking individual infection histories, migration, and clinical data with validated TB outcomes.
